venue_now: preprint: header 'Preprint. Under review.' and arXiv 2504.06260v1, 8 Apr 2025 (p.1); no venue in the text
what_it_is: FEABench evaluates LLMs and LLM agents on solving physics, mathematics and engineering problems with finite element analysis, by generating Java API calls that drive COMSOL Multiphysics (pp.1-2). FEABench Gold has 15 manually verified problems derived from COMSOL Application Gallery tutorials, each with model specifications, selection information, a step-by-step plan, a target value, ground-truth API code and a model tree; FEABench Large has 200 algorithmically parsed tutorial tasks with no verifiable numeric target (pp.2-3). Scoring combines executability, model-tree similarity to the ground truth, physics-interface factuality, interface, feature and feature-property recall against the ground-truth code, feature dimension, and target relative error (pp.5-6). Six LLMs were tested at baseline, the best computing a valid target for 1 of 15 problems, and a multi-turn agent raises executability from 0.62 to 0.88 (pp.6-7, 9).
domain: engineering simulation (multiphysics finite element analysis), e.g. heat transfer and structural mechanics, plus a Black-Scholes option model and quantum-dot eigenfrequency analysis (p.3)
size: 15 Gold problems (each in two task versions, ModelSpecs and Plan) plus 200 Large tasks; a 768-snippet annotated library used only for retrieval, not evaluation (pp.2-3); 6 LLMs at baseline and one agent (pp.6-9)
source_of_items: derived from COMSOL Application Gallery tutorials: 2-3 problems annotated by an expert COMSOL user, the rest drafted by an LLM from the tutorials, then corrected and verified by humans (pp.3, 15); the Large set parsed algorithmically (p.3)
has_gold_traces: partial: each Gold problem has a step-by-step natural-language plan for the software, ground-truth API code and a model tree, i.e. a reference solution path made of software actions, not a worked derivation (p.3)
evaluation: code- and execution-based intermediate metrics against the ground-truth code (executability, model-tree score, physics-interface factuality, interface/feature/feature-property recall, feature dimension) plus target relative error, for which an LLM checks that the exported value is a valid target and a 'strict' cut requires an error under 10% (pp.5-6, Table 1)
human_validation: Gold problems were manually confirmed to be self-sufficient and solvable, with the ground-truth code checked to export the target value (pp.2, 15). I found no human validation of the metrics or of the LLM validity check.
contamination_measures: none reported; the problems derive from public COMSOL tutorials available online (pp.3, 10)

engtrace_use.sentence: S-E2 (L190-198): 'Others focus on tangential skills such as design generation (Guo et al., 2025b) or software proficiency (Mudur et al., 2025), while broader efforts like EngiBench (Zhou et al., 2025) rely on subjective rubric-based scoring.' S-I3c (L116-122): 'EngTrace addresses both gaps through integrative reasoning templates that, unlike existing benchmarks (e.g., Zhou et al., 2025; Mudur et al., 2025) that rely solely on outcome matching, demand holistic procedural reasoning'. Also covered by S-E3 (L199-205): 'existing benchmarks remain limited to outcome matching'.
engtrace_use.explanation: The overall verdict is the worst of the three. S-E2, imprecise: FEABench does test operating FEA software through its API, and the paper finds translating modelling decisions into valid API calls a bigger bottleneck than making the decisions (p.8). But its stated aim is multiphysics reasoning combined with operating simulation software: it lists correct physics decisions (boundary conditions, material properties, spatial dimensions) among the skills it tests (p.2) and scores them with dedicated physics metrics (p.6), so 'software proficiency' as a 'tangential skill' undersells it. S-I3c, wrong: FEABench explicitly does not rely solely on outcome matching. It introduces 'a holistic automated evaluation strategy with intermediate metrics that seek to measure different facets of distance to a correct solution' (p.2), including a model-tree score that 'measures the alignment of the model's solution path with a successful path' and recall of physics interfaces and features against the ground-truth code (p.6). Most of its reported results come from these metrics, because almost no solution computes a valid target (0 or 1 of 15 at baseline; Table 2, p.7). S-E3, wrong for this paper for the same reason. The two May framings are also incompatible with each other (citation map C7).

suggested_wording: FEABench (Mudur et al., 2025) has models and agents solve multiphysics problems by writing COMSOL Multiphysics API calls and, besides the computed target value, scores intermediate artifacts against ground-truth code, such as model-tree similarity and recall of physics features, on 15 manually verified problems drawn from software tutorials.
facts_to_cite: The task is to solve physics, mathematics and engineering problems end to end with finite element analysis, by generating Java API calls to COMSOL Multiphysics (pp.1-2)
FEABench Gold: 15 manually verified problems from COMSOL Application Gallery tutorials; FEABench Large: 200 algorithmically parsed tutorial tasks without a verifiable numeric target (pp.2-3)
Each Gold entry has model specifications, selection information, a step-by-step plan, the target value, ground-truth API code and a model tree (p.3)

Metrics: executability, model-tree score against the ground truth, physics-interface factuality, interface/feature/feature-property recall, feature dimension, and target relative error with an LLM validity check and a 10% strict cut (pp.5-6, Table 1)
The skills it names are low-resource code generation, inferring spatial dimensions and geometry, and correct physics decisions such as boundary conditions and material properties (p.2)
At baseline, the best of six LLMs (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) computes a valid target for 1 of 15 problems (Table 2, p.7)

A multi-turn agent with tools and execution feedback raises executability from 0.62 to 0.88 and computes a valid target for 2 of 15 (Table 5, p.9); the one value that passed the strict cut was COMSOL's default temperature (20 C against a target of 18.3 C), which the authors read as a sign the problem was not truly solved (p.9)
The paper finds translating decisions into valid API calls a larger bottleneck than making correct modelling decisions (p.8)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: physics and engineering problems with numeric targets; credit for intermediate progress measured against a reference solution (ground-truth code and model tree), the nearest thing in this batch to EngTrace's milestone checks; manual verification of every Gold problem. Lacks: generated instances (15 static, tutorial-derived problems); a gold reasoning trace in EngTrace's sense (its reference path is a sequence of software actions, not a derivation whose intermediate quantities can be checked); any evaluation of the model's own written reasoning; expert validation of the evaluator; any contamination measure, although the tutorials are public. The output is code for a commercial solver, so the skill tested differs from EngTrace's worked solutions.
notes: The May text uses FEABench in two incompatible ways ('software proficiency' in S-E2, an outcome-matching benchmark in S-I3c), and both undersell it: its title claims multiphysics reasoning and it scores intermediate artifacts. EngiBench (Zhou et al., 2025) itself classes FEABench as 'task-oriented' evaluation (zhou2025engibench, p.3). The text is v1, under review; a later version or venue may exist, which I could not check without the web. The execution-based metrics need a COMSOL licence (p.10).
